title: AI spending boom out of puff, says Macquarie
full_text:
The great artificial-intelligence investment boom that has underpinned global growth for the best part of two years is starting to run out of puff, Macquarie warns.
Just as the AI build-out had become more dependent on external funding markets, the Federal Reserve’s resumption of interest rate increases has made it harder for the AI “enabler” companies to raise the money needed to keep building at the current pace, Macquarie equity strategist Matthew Brooks says.
Brooks points to a string of warning signs: two planned stockmarket listings of data-centre companies – Firmus and AirTrunk – have been pulled; credit markets are showing wider concerns about funding; and a basket of so-called “AI enabler” stocks – the chipmakers, power suppliers and infrastructure builders riding the boom – has broken below key moving averages.
“The Fed hike lifted the cost of capital just as the AI build became more dependent on external funding,” Brooks says.
Add Nscale to the list. The Nvidia-backed data centre developer is reportedly now facing opposition to the valuation target it is pursuing in its initial public offering.
Nscale has been seeking an IPO valuation of about $US30bn ($43bn). But a cohort of investors lately have urged that a valuation in the $US16bn-$US19bn range would be more likely to find favour with buyers, in light of factors including the implosion of Australian AI data centre company Firmus’s IPO plan, according to media reports.
A disconnect over valuation would add to recent challenges facing London-based Nscale’s planned IPO, after Microsoft – one of the company’s biggest customers – pulled out of a UK data centre deal with Nscale, it said on Sunday, with the site contending with delays from power constraints.
At a local Citi conference on Tuesday, AirTrunk predicted that the AI-driven data centre boom would moderate due to the rising cost of credit and power supply challenges amid more investor scrutiny over developers’ track record in building facilities.
Macquarie’s Brooks says a negative capex surprise from any of the hyperscalers would confirm his view that there is already enough evidence to expect slower AI capex growth in 2027.
Here’s where it gets interesting for Australian investors. Brooks expects bond markets to start pricing in the risk of weaker AI spending well before the Reserve Bank is ready to cut interest rates.
That matters because his firm’s own measure of RBA tone is now sitting at its most hawkish level in the 20-year history of the series.
Rather than seeing that as a reason for rates to keep rising, he reads it the other way.
“The case for a pause is growing as consumer and business confidence weaken and unemployment rises,” he says, predicting that the central bank’s language is more likely to soften from here than harden further.
Brooks and his team have done some historical detective work to figure out which sectors and stocks tend to do best as this kind of scenario unfolds.
They looked at 12 previous episodes in which Australian bond yields fell by more than one percentage point, as well as all eight RBA rate-cutting cycles since 1990.
The pattern that emerges is fairly clear.
Infrastructure, property trusts and healthcare stocks tend to perform best in the early stages, as yields fall but before the RBA actually starts cutting. That’s because they combine long-term earnings with a degree of defensiveness – useful if the economy is also slowing.
“Property is particularly attractive now,” Brooks notes.
But he cautions that it tends to lose momentum once actual cuts begin and investors start chasing more cyclical recovery plays. Retailers and housing-linked companies only really come into their own once rate cuts are locked in and confidence in lower borrowing costs builds.
On the stock front, Macquarie recently flagged toll-road operator Transurban as a standout performer in previous episodes of falling yields, along with property groups GPT and Mirvac.
The broker now adds building products maker James Hardie to its model portfolio, arguing that if US data-centre spending slows, it should also pull down US mortgage rates – a direct benefit for the Hardie business. It has removed insurer Challenger from the portfolio, noting the stock has historically lagged both as yields fall and after rate cuts begin.
Resources and energy stocks, by contrast, have generally underperformed through both stages of the cycle in Macquarie’s analysis, and the broker suggests investors could fund their rotation into the preferred sectors by trimming exposure there.
Brooks is careful to note this isn’t a call that AI itself is finished. Rather, he sees it as the investment cycle cooling before the technology’s adoption does – which, in his view, could ultimately help bring down the cost of the technology ahead of a broader rollout.
The next test, he says, is whether weaker momentum in AI-related shares spreads into actual capital spending plans, commodity prices and global bond yields more broadly. For now, Macquarie’s advice to investors is to lean into quality, yield-sensitive stocks while the froth comes out of the AI trade – and be ready to rotate into retailers and housing-exposed names once the RBA actually starts cutting rates.
